title: Changing Tables With ALTER and DROP
summary: Add, rename, retype, and remove columns, and drop tables.
intro: Real tables change after they are created: a new feature needs a column, an old one goes away, a name turns out wrong. `ALTER TABLE` changes a table in place and keeps its rows, and `DROP TABLE` removes a table you no longer need.

steps.title: Adding and removing columns
steps.body:
This lesson changes a `customers` table whose sign-up dates were stored as text by mistake. There is also an unused `old_customers` table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name text,
    phone text,
    signed_up text
);
-- ('Ana Lopez', '555-0101', '2025-03-01'), ('Ben Carter', '555-0102', '2025-03-14'), ...
CREATE TABLE old_customers (id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, full_name text);
```

`ALTER TABLE` changes a table and keeps its rows. Each change prints `ALTER TABLE`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN email text;
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN phone;
```

A new column goes at the end and is NULL in every existing row. Add a `DEFAULT` and the existing rows get that value too. That matters for `NOT NULL`: `ADD COLUMN points integer NOT NULL` fails on a table with rows, because they would all be NULL:

```text
ERROR:  column "points" of relation "customers" contains null values
```

`ADD COLUMN points integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` works.

`DROP COLUMN` deletes the column and its data for good, with no undo.

To see a table's columns, query `information_schema.columns`, a built-in table with one row per column. `ordinal_position` is the column's place in the table:

```sql
SELECT column_name, data_type
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'customers'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
```

example.title: Loyalty points instead of phones
example.prompt: Add a loyalty_points column that starts at 0, drop the phone column, then list the columns and the rows.

----------------+-----------

 signed_up      | text

(4 rows)

 id | full_name  | signed_up  | loyalty_points
----+------------+------------+----------------
  1 | Ana Lopez  | 2025-03-01 |              0
  2 | Ben Carter | 2025-03-14 |              0
  3 | Chloe Kim  | 2025-04-02 |              0
  4 | Dev Patel  | 2025-04-20 |              0
(4 rows)
example.explanation: The `DEFAULT 0` fills `loyalty_points` for the four existing rows, which is what lets `NOT NULL` pass. Dropping `phone` removes it from every row. The column list shows the new column last, because `ADD COLUMN` always appends, and `SELECT *` follows that same order.

steps.title: Renaming and changing types
steps.body:
Renames keep every row and only change the name:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN full_name TO name;
ALTER TABLE customers RENAME TO clients;
```

After a rename, queries that use the old name fail, so update them too.

`ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` changes a column's type. Text to date has no automatic cast, so add `USING` with the expression that converts each row's old value:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN signed_up TYPE date USING signed_up::date;
```

Without `USING` you get this error:

```text
ERROR:  column "signed_up" cannot be cast automatically to type date
```

With `USING`, one row that cannot convert (like `'soon'`) fails the whole statement and nothing changes.

`SET NOT NULL` adds a rule to an existing column, and fails if any row is already NULL there. `SET DEFAULT` sets the value later inserts get when they leave the column out. Unlike `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT`, it does not touch existing rows. `DROP NOT NULL` and `DROP DEFAULT` undo them:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN full_name SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET DEFAULT 'new';
```

In `information_schema.columns`, the `is_nullable` column shows `YES` or `NO`.

example.title: Real sign-up dates
example.prompt: Rename full_name to name, turn signed_up into a real date that is required, list the columns, and show when each 30 day trial ends.
example.output:
ALTER TABLE

ALTER TABLE

ALTER TABLE

 column_name | data_type | is_nullable
-------------+-----------+-------------
 id          | integer   | NO
 name        | text      | YES
 phone       | text      | YES
 signed_up   | date      | NO
(4 rows)

    name    | signed_up  | trial_ends
------------+------------+------------
 Ana Lopez  | 2025-03-01 | 2025-03-31
 Ben Carter | 2025-03-14 | 2025-04-13
 Chloe Kim  | 2025-04-02 | 2025-05-02
 Dev Patel  | 2025-04-20 | 2025-05-20
(4 rows)
example.explanation: `USING signed_up::date` casts each row's text, so `signed_up` becomes a date and the data stays. The column list now shows `name`, the `date` type, and `NO` under `is_nullable` for `signed_up` and the primary key `id`. Because `signed_up` is a date, `signed_up + 30` adds 30 days. On the old text column it would have been an error.

steps.title: Dropping tables safely
steps.body:
`DROP TABLE` deletes a table, its rows and all, and prints `DROP TABLE`. There is no undo, so check the name first:

```sql
DROP TABLE old_customers;
```

Dropping a table that does not exist is an error:

```text
ERROR:  table "archive" does not exist
```

Add `IF EXISTS` and the statement does nothing when the table is missing, which makes cleanup scripts safe to run twice. `DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS` works the same way for columns:

```sql
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS archive;
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS fax;
```

A table that another table's foreign key points at cannot be dropped while that link exists:

```text
ERROR:  cannot drop table customers because other objects depend on it
```

Drop the child table first, then the parent.

To list your tables, query `information_schema.tables`. Your tables live in the `public` schema, while PostgreSQL's own tables live in other schemas, so filter on `table_schema`:

```sql
SELECT table_name
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public'
ORDER BY table_name;
```

example.title: Clearing out old tables
example.prompt: Drop old_customers, safely drop an archive table and a fax column that may not exist, then list the tables.
example.output:
DROP TABLE

DROP TABLE

ALTER TABLE

 table_name
------------
 customers
(1 row)
example.explanation: `old_customers` exists, so it is dropped. `archive` and the `fax` column never existed, but `IF EXISTS` turns those statements into no-ops that still print their tags. The table list shows only `customers` left in `public`.

practice.title: A scratch table
practice.prompt:
Create a scratch table, clean up with DROP, and list the tables that are left.

1. Create a table `import_rows` with columns `line_number` (integer) and `raw_line` (text).
2. Drop `import_rows`.
3. Drop the table `backups` with `IF EXISTS`. It does not exist.
4. Drop the column `email` from `customers` with `IF EXISTS`. It does not exist.
5. Select `table_name` from `information_schema.tables` where `table_schema` is `'public'`, sorted by `table_name`.

Expected output:

```text
CREATE TABLE

DROP TABLE

DROP TABLE

ALTER TABLE

  table_name
---------------
 customers
 old_customers
(2 rows)
```

hints: A plain `DROP TABLE` works on `import_rows`, because it exists by then.
`IF EXISTS` goes right after `DROP TABLE` or `DROP COLUMN`, before the name.
Dropping a column is a change to its table, so it starts with `ALTER TABLE customers`.

recap:
- `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c type DEFAULT v` adds a column, and the default fills existing rows.
- `DROP COLUMN c` and `DROP TABLE t` delete data for good. `IF EXISTS` skips what is missing.
- `RENAME COLUMN a TO b` and `RENAME TO new_name` keep the rows.
- `ALTER COLUMN c TYPE type USING expression` converts each row's value.
- `ALTER COLUMN c SET NOT NULL` and `SET DEFAULT v` change a column's rules. `SET DEFAULT` only affects later inserts.
- `information_schema.columns` and `information_schema.tables` describe your tables.
